paras: The police beating of George Sewell took place on the night of Sunday, August 6, 1905, when Patrolman Patrick J. Carmody, off duty and in plain clothes, beat Sewell, a young Black man, with his revolver while arresting him on West 28th Street in New York City. Magistrate Pool of the West Side court discharged Sewell and held the policeman in $1,000 bail for felonious assault, saying he had struck Sewell because he was Black.

Sewell, given as 18, 20 or 21 years old, lived at 414 West 28th Street and had worked for five years for William H. Fowler, who called him "very obedient, polite and useful." Carmody belonged to the West 37th Street station.

Late on the Sunday night a mattress was burning in the street near Sewell's home. Carmody told the court that Sewell, whom he accused of setting the fire, knocked him into the gutter and jumped on him, and that he struck the youth twice with his revolver butt in self-defence. Sewell testified instead that he was only watching the fire, did not know the plainclothes man was a policeman, and saw him push a revolver into the face of a neighbor, Fred Ellis, before falling on Sewell in the gutter. Fearing he would be killed, Sewell said, he cried for mercy, and was then beaten with the pistol at intervals all the way to the station. In court the next morning his eyebrow was torn loose, his scalp cut and his face swollen, while the Sun noted that Carmody "hadn't a scratch on him."

Arraigned on August 7 for violating a corporation ordinance and assaulting the officer, Sewell was held in $500 bail, which Fowler furnished, after breaking away from Carmody in court and crying that the policeman would beat him again. At the examination the next day an Italian barber, Alfred Sprogna, Ellis, and Mrs. Abbie Tenbrook, a white neighbor, corroborated Sewell, and Tenbrook said Carmody had threatened to blow her head off when she screamed. Carmody admitted he had been off duty and armed; Pool refused him an adjournment, discharged Sewell and ordered him held.

Captain Dennis Ward protested that the officer had not had "a square deal" and was ordered from the bridge. According to the New York Age, the case went to District Attorney Jerome for the grand jury; no later report of grand jury action or a trial appears in the coverage. The Sun then published police records showing 34 complaints against Carmody since 1894, and Fowler said he would take the matter to the Police Commissioner.

The Colored Republican Club passed resolutions commending Pool, and an Age reporter thanked him on behalf of the paper, "the Afro-American citizens of New York" and the Colored Citizens' Protective League. Pool replied that police beatings of citizens "simply because of their color" were a growing evil that he would punish.

New York's white dailies treated the case as court news, under headlines such as the Evening World's "Negro Feared Beating," the Sun's "Cried Out That Cop Beat Him" and the Tribune's "Orders Patrolman Arrested." The Tribune and Sun gave much of their space to Pool's quarrel with Ward, and a letter to the Sun praised Pool's handling of "the recent case of police brutality" while its writer declared himself "no champion of the negro." Outside New York, the Louisville Courier-Journal reprinted an Evening Post item on Carmody's record on August 15.

The New York Age ran the story on its front page on August 17 as "Daniel Come to Judgment," praising Pool's "courageous action" and calling the officer "about three sheets in the wind." Where the Sun reported Pool's remark about race as a question Carmody denied, the Age printed it as a finding that he hit Sewell "because he was black"; the Age also named the officer Connody or Connolly and gave his prior charges as 24.

Carmody said Sewell and other young colored boys set the fire, while Tenbrook and the Age blamed Italian children, and Sewell denied it. The Sun placed the fire at 406 West 28th Street, the Age near 25th Street and Ninth Avenue.

bases: An off-duty policeman beat Sewell with his revolver while arresting him and taking him to the station, and was charged with felonious assault (A3, A4, A10).

The Evening World, Sun, Tribune and New York Age independently report the beating and Pool's ruling, and the officer himself admitted striking Sewell twice with his revolver butt, though he claimed self-defence (A1, A2, A3, A4, A10).

accounts.label: Officer Carmody
accounts.gist: He found a mattress burning, accused Sewell of starting it, and Sewell cursed him, knocked him into the gutter and jumped on him; he struck Sewell twice with his revolver butt in self-defence and had 'no chance' to show his shield.

accounts.label: Sewell and witnesses
accounts.gist: Sewell was only watching the fire, did not know the plainclothes man was a policeman, was struck with a revolver and beaten in the gutter and then all the way to the station; three witnesses corroborated him and one said Carmody threatened to shoot her.

accounts.label: Magistrate Pool
accounts.gist: Pool rejected the officer's account, discharged Sewell, held Carmody for felonious assault and said he had hit Sewell because he was Black.

framing.detail: The Sun's 'Cried Out That Cop Beat Him' contrasted Sewell's torn eyebrow with Carmody's unmarked face, and its follow-up published Carmody's disciplinary record.
The Evening World ('Negro Feared Beating') and Tribune ('Orders Patrolman Arrested') reported the hearings as court news, the Tribune stressing the magistrate's clash with Captain Ward.
A Sun letter writer praised Pool's handling of 'police brutality' while declaring himself 'no champion of the negro'.
The New York Age's 'Daniel Come to Judgment' called the clubbing brutal, praised Pool's 'courageous action', and reported Black organizations' thanks.
